newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks end sharply lower prior to jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks end sharply lower prior to jobs data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed sharply lower Thursday on worries that Friday's employment report for August might spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 49.94 points at 5,606.96. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,587 to 749 on moderate volume of 360 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It's a waiting game. The signs are the economy is stronger than we expected, which means earnings will be good, but the Fed could tighten," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management.

Analysts said the market feared the jobs report will show that the economy spawned a large number of jobs and that the data may prod the Fed to raise interest rates at the Sept. 24 meeting of its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
Wall Street will focus on average hourly earnings. Hourly earnings jumped by 9 cents in June -- the largest gain since the government's record-keeping began 31 years ago.
The Fed has kept interest rates unchanged since it last cut them in January by one-quarter of a percentage point.
Economists surveyed by Reuters are calling for a gain of 244,000 non-farm jobs in August compared with a rise of 193,000 in July.

Analysts said the market may have gotten a taste of what to expect in Friday's monthly jobs numbers as the Labour Department reported that new applications for unemployment benefits fell by an unexpectedly sharp 15,000 last week, ending four straight weeks of rises.
The jobless claims for the week ended Aug. 31 fell to 316,000 from 331,000 in the prior week. They had been expected at about 335,000.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond was off 20/32 and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, rose to 7.15 percent from 7.10 percent at Wednesday's close.
"The last few days have shown stocks can't make upward progress when the long bond yield is over 7 percent," said UBS Securities Chief Investment Strategist Gail Dudack.
Financial stocks bore the brunt of the interest-rate fuelled sell-off. J.P. Morgan & Co. fell 1-5/8 to 87 and BankAmerica Corp. lost 1-1/8 to 77-1/8.
Comments by two Fed officials sharpened the market's focus on Friday's report, although their remarks did little to signal the near-term outlook for Fed policy.
Speaking in Houston, Dallas Fed President Robert McTeer said the economy was "running hot," although he also noted that indicators he watched showed little threat of inflation.
Later, Fed Gov. Janet Yellen said she expected demand growth to moderate to a more sustainable pace during the rest of 1996 and into 1997.
Yellen balanced that comment by saying that it was "too soon to tell for sure whether wage pressures presented too much of an upside risk to the economy."

Meanwhile, stocks did pick up one vote of confidence from Fidelity Investments' Magellan fund as the nation's largest mutual fund boosted its stock holdings and reduced its holdings of both bonds and cash.
Fidelity also said the fund's assets rose to $51.91 billion as of Sept. 4 from $50.97 billion at the end of July.

American depositary shares in Russian companies fell on news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had agreed to undergo heart surgery. Templeton Russia Fund, the only closed-end fund on the NYSE that invests exclusively in Russian companies, fell 3/4 to 20-7/8.
A number of retail stocks struggled throughout the session on disappointing monthly sales reports.
Gap Inc., which reported flat same-store sales fell 4-7/8 to 29. Kmart Corp. fell 3/8 to 9-7/8. The company reported a 1 percent increase in August sales and said its performance remained below plan.
Zilog Inc. tumbled 8-3/8 to 15-1/2 after warning its third quarter earnings per share would fall well short of second quarter levels.
Campbell Soup Co. surged 4-1/8 to 71-5/8 after announcing it would buy back a total of $2.5 billion of its shares and undertake a consolidation and restructuring plan.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 18.16 points to 1,125.66.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was down 6.17 to 649.44. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.63 to 556.71.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 2.73 to 349.64. The average share was down 30 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,394.66, down 60.137 or 0.93 percent.
